articles.title: Veteran shot 7 times in Fort Hood massacre has a warning for Americans planning to watch execution
articles.summary: A Fort Hood shooting survivor shot seven times by Nidal Hasan wants to witness the firing squad execution but warns against treating it as a spectacle.
articles.body:
On Dec. 3, 2026, the U.S. government intends to take Nidal Hasan to a firing range at Fort Hood and publicly execute him.

Few condemned men could make a more difficult case for mercy.

Seventeen years ago, Hasan, an Army psychiatrist at the time, walked into a soldier readiness center at the Texas Army post and opened fire, killing 13 people and wounding 32 others. Now, after years of appeals, the Army is preparing to execute him by firing squad.

And Americans will be able to watch on live stream.

That last detail has transformed what might otherwise have been the long-delayed conclusion of one of the darkest chapters in the Army's history into a more uncomfortable question: How should a nation reckon with the gravity of taking a life, even when that life belongs to a mass murderer?

For Alonzo Lunsford, a former Army staff sergeant who survived being shot seven times by Hasan, the answer is complicated.

Lunsford wants Hasan executed. He intends to witness it himself in December. He told Fox News Digital he would even prefer that one of Hasan's surviving victims or the relatives of those he killed be allowed to pull the trigger.

Despite that, Lunsford says he has forgiven Hasan.

"The weird thing about it, I've forgiven him because my faith does not allow me to heal and continue unless I forgive that man," Lunsford said.

But forgiveness, for Lunsford, does not mean sparing Hasan from punishment. What troubles him is the prospect of turning that punishment into entertainment.

"It's not a spectacle," he said. "There's nothing glorified in the smell of human flesh, blood and gunpowder. It's a smell you will never forget. It's a taste that you will never forget."

"That's not something you sit around and say, hey, let's get some popcorn and look at this execution," he continued. "We as a people, we're better than that. This ain't no country where we do public beheadings and stonings and think it's fine."

Lunsford was working at Fort Hood's Soldier Readiness Processing Center on Nov. 5, 2009, when Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, opened fire. He recalled watching Hasan kill a colleague before turning the weapon on him. Lunsford was shot above his left eye, fell to the floor and played dead before eventually escaping outside, where Hasan shot him again.

"I've accepted the fact I'm gonna live with the pain for the rest of my life," Lunsford said.

He has since found purpose in coaching basketball, mentoring young people and helping others struggling with their mental health.

Lunsford said he doesn't want children watching the livestream, though he believes adults can decide for themselves whether to tune in.

"This is not somewhere you all start throwing some meat on the grill, get outside and say, hey, we're gonna watch them unalive this guy by firing squad," he said. "Don't do that."

"Don't do that because when you do that, you're dishonoring those that made the supreme sacrifice, those who are no longer here. Those are heroes."

War Secretary Pete Hegseth has defended making the execution public, saying Americans should understand the consequences of Hasan's crimes.

"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Hegseth said in an interview this week. "Because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things."

Vice President JD Vance cast doubt Friday on whether the Pentagon would follow through with its plans to livestream Hasan's execution , saying he had no intention of watching it himself.

"I see these announcements. I don't know that that's actually going to happen," he told reporters Friday.

The decision for the first U.S. Army death by firing squad in 86 years to be live streamed has drawn opposition even from Republicans who support putting Hasan to death .

"I absolutely support the sentence of death, but live-streaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that," Rep. Austin Scott, R-Ga., wrote on X.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., likewise said Hasan "should face the death penalty," but called publicly streaming it "beyond disgusting."

"Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do," Tillis wrote. "It should not be happening in America."

The nation's Catholic bishops have gone further, opposing both Hasan's execution and the decision to make it public. "In no way can Hassan's actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered," Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, said Friday.

"The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people."

The decision has also raised a more immediate national security concern.

Hasan, who was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot during the 2009 attack, has previously spoken about becoming a martyr. Matthew Levitt, a former Treasury counterterrorism official and director of the Washington Institute's Reinhard Program on Counterterrorism and Intelligence, warned that making footage of his death widely available could give terrorist groups material to exploit.

"It seems like a poor decision to provide terrorist groups with a video clip they can effectively splice into radicalization propaganda," Levitt told Fox News Digital.

"There's no tangible benefit to live streaming an execution , and it may, in fact, exacerbate the terrorist threat."

For Lunsford, however, the execution remains deeply personal.

During Hasan's 2013 court-martial, the two locked eyes. Lunsford wants Hasan to see him again before he dies.

"I want to look at him in his eyes. I want him to see me — man to man," Lunsford said. "My message to him: Dude, you failed."

"I go where I wanna go, when I wanna go, how I wanna go. With no fear," he said. "I can go outside and just smell and listen to nature. You don't have that luxury."

And despite everything Hasan took from him, Lunsford said he hopes the condemned man uses his final moments to repent.

"I want to give him the opportunity to, the last words out of his mouth is to apologize and repent," Lunsford said. "And be held accountable for his sins and for his crime. And I will be OK with that."

articles.title: Deflating engineered discontent
articles.summary: The CJP, the SIR, and the Anatomy of a Protest That Cannot End The Cockroach Janta Party is back in the heart of the capital.
articles.body: The CJP, the SIR, and the Anatomy of a Protest That Cannot EndThe Cockroach Janta Party is back in the heart of the capital. This time the target is not a minister, but the referee of Indian democracy itself. On October 10, the youth-led movement that forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation in July, attempted its “Jantar Mantar 2.0,” demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The immediate trigger is real and specific. A September 23 Indian Express investigation revealed that two Election Commissioners had formally objected at least 14 times over ten months to decisions taken by the poll panel under Gyanesh Kumar. Some of these decisions, the two commissioners said, were taken without their knowledge. Since the SIR began in Bihar in June 2025 and expanded nationwide, more than 130 million names have been removed from draft voter lists.The CJP’s demands have hardened accordingly: Kumar’s resignation and a criminal investigation, a halt to SIR exclusions, restoration of the January 2025 electoral rolls pending verification, transfer of the relevant records to the Supreme Court or an independent judicial inquiry, repeal of the 2023 law governing the appointment of election commissioners, and a boycott of elections altogether so long as Kumar remains in office. The Election Commission denies wrongdoing, insisting that operational queries raised during drafting are standard practice and that all SIR decisions were taken unanimously by the three-member body.The mobilisation has spread. A CJP rally at Mumbai’s Shivaji Park and protests at Jantar Mantar on October 2 (Gandhi Jayanti) were followed by an INDI Alliance march to the Election Commission on October 6, at which Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and other opposition MPs were detained. The CJP’s October 10 call drew student groups, civil-society organisations, farmer bodies and a coalition of opposition parties.Everything now unfolding in Delhi follows a pattern that has become unmistakable. It has repeated, almost to the letter.The goalposts keep changing. The CJP began with exam paper leaks and the demand for a minister’s scalp. It moved from “fix the exams” to “sack the minister” to “apologise to students” to “compensation for suicide families” to “withdraw all FIRs.” Pradhan resigned. Within 48 hours, the movement had found a new front. Now the grievance has migrated from the examination system to the electoral roll, from a minister to the Chief Election Commissioner. Each resolution opens a new front; each concession becomes the platform for the next demand. The issue changes; the structure does not.The movement has no ability to effect closure. It is leaderless, decentralised, horizontally organised. This is a strategic strength: with no head to strike, the state cannot decapitate it. But it is also a structural disability: with no leadership that can negotiate or sign, there is no mechanism to accept a settlement. Every demand met is reframed as insufficient; every victory is treated as a down-payment. The July experience proved this when a protest permitted for one day ran for a month.Political actors enter and make hay with the confusion. In Delhi and Mumbai, AAP leaders, the Left and its student wings (AISA and SFI), NSUI, Congress, RJD, Shiv Sena (UBT) and MNS leaders all attached themselves to a movement that was not theirs. Uddhav Thackeray and Raj Thackeray led the Mumbai march; Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra were detained at the Election Commission march. They compete to own the agitation while it suits them, and they have every incentive not to let it close, because a simmering grievance is a permanent campaign platform.Also Read| The students deserved justice. India deserves reformIt is not in their interest to allow closure. A resolved grievance is a lost opportunity. A simmering one is an annuity.This is not uniquely Indian. In Kenya, the Finance Bill was withdrawn and the cabinet sacked, yet protests continued. In Bangladesh, the quota was cut, yet the movement escalated to regime change. In Nepal, Peru and Indonesia, the same dynamics played out. The grievance changes with the country; the anatomy is the same.The police are handed a task that has no clean answer. Having watched the last protest break its own undertakings when a one-day permission that ran for a month, more than 200 police personnel injured, thousands with criminal antecedents in the crowd, women constables molested, the security apparatus this time took no chances. It shut central Delhi down.The reasoning is not irrational. Jantar Mantar holds about a thousand people; the CJP claimed it would bring twenty thousand. Constitutional bodies such as the Election Commission and Parliament sit in New Delhi. The police argue they have a duty to residents, commuters and the economy of a capital that cannot be halted for every protest, and that permission is not anti-democratic but a mechanism to plan for safety, traffic and emergency access.But the crackdown carries its own cost. When a state shuts 45 metro stations, suspends mobile internet, cancels 200 trains and detains hundreds, it converts a protest about democratic legitimacy into a spectacle of democratic foreclosure. It creates exactly the grievance it claims to contain. The Supreme Court’s warning, do not use a hammer to kill a fly, captures the trap precisely.But one feels for the police. They are damned if they do and damned if they don’t. Allow the protest, and if a fraction of the crowd turns violent, the state is blamed for the disorder, while the movement gains its martyrs. Prevent it, and the state is blamed for authoritarianism and the movement gains its grievance. Either way, the movement grows. The police are being asked to solve, with barricades and batons, a problem that is not a law-and-order problem at all. It is a political one.How, then, can any of this be controlled?The answer rests on a single core insight: the cycle of simmering discontent survives because three things are true at once. The structural grievance is real, the movement has no mechanism to accept closure, and political actors benefit from keeping it alive. A counter-strategy must work on all three fronts simultaneously. No single move is sufficient.The first step must be to acknowledge the real grievance. The voter-roll question is not invented. Fourteen repeated internal objections, 130 million names removed, and a genuine loss of public trust in the Election Commission are real. The government’s first move should be to say so, in its own voice, rather than leading with conspiracy allegations. India’s Supreme Court itself advised during the NEET protests: “Listen to Gen Z, do not repress them… The most powerful resource is reasoning.” Acknowledgment denies the opposition the monopoly on speaking for the voter. But it must be followed immediately by substance. A purely rhetorical acknowledgment that fixes nothing is worse than silence, because it confirms that only pressure works.Then, don’t be reactive. Reactive government loses. Each time the movement raises a new demand, the state scrambles. The counter is to proactively announce a comprehensive package that addresses not just the current demand but the ones the movement will inevitably escalate to: an independent audit of the SIR, restoration timelines, judicial supervision of the roll revision, and the question of the appointment law. The UNDP’s protest-response framework calls this creating “institutional mechanisms to process demands”. Without them, mobilisations produce greater frustration and, potentially, violence. If you concede at peak momentum, you credit the protest; if you concede early and comprehensively, you credit governance. The same concession, timed differently, produces opposite political outcomes.Also, Fix the structure, not the symbol. A Chief Election Commissioner’s resignation without electoral-roll reform is a scalp that emboldens the next movement. Across the global wave, the recurring failure is symbolic concession with the structure left intact.Also Read| NEET protests: A double tragedy for students and a warning for the systemMake reform verifiable. Gen Z are digital natives who do not rely on mainstream media; their understanding is shaped by platforms, peer networks and first-hand experience. They are hard to gaslight and hard to satisfy with press releases. Proactive information sharing builds trust, while withholding creates suspicion. If the government is genuinely fixing the roll, transparency becomes its strongest defence, not press conferences, not IT-cell counter-narratives, but verifiable data.Do not feed the martyr machine. Every crackdown creates new grievances that become new demands.The UN Model Protocol is clear: states should foster a climate that respects and promotes the right to peaceful assembly.Build institutional channels so the street is not the only venue. If the only way to be heard is street protest, street protest recurs. In Thailand, the Gen Z movement converted its protest energy into a political party that won the most seats in 2023, and the street energy subsided because there was an institutional channel. In Bangladesh, where no such channel existed, the movement escalated until it toppled the government. Result? The youth found themselves iced out of the transition. Give them a seat at the table before they overturn the table.Expose political manipulation, but first, establish credibility. The instinct to lead with foreign-funding and conspiracy allegations before establishing credibility on the substance backfires. It looks like deflection, and the opposition dismisses it as a predictable template. If the funding is genuinely illicit, prove it through due process and prove it after fixing the real grievance, not before. The sequencing is critical: first acknowledge the genuine grievance, then announce structural reform, then, having established credibility, transparently investigate and expose manipulation through proper institutional channels. Accommodate first on the genuine grievance; confront the manipulation second, not the reverse.As said earlier, the cycle survives because three things are true at once: the structural grievance is real, the movement has no mechanism to accept closure, and political actors benefit from keeping it alive. You cannot address only one. If you fix the structure but do not build institutional channels, the next trigger produces the next eruption. If you build channels but do not fix the structure, the channels lose credibility. If you do both but do not expose the manipulation, the manipulators keep engineering new triggers. The counter-strategy has to work on all three fronts simultaneously: resolve the structural grievance visibly and verifiably, build institutional channels so protest is not the only path, and expose political manipulation through credible institutional processes after establishing your own credibility on the real issue. No single move is sufficient. The combination is what breaks the cycle.A republic that can only answer a protest with a lockdown, and a protest that can only answer a concession with a new demand, are trapped in the same loop. The way out is not more barricades or more hashtags. It is to make the grievance real, the reform visible, and the channel open.The movement must have somewhere to go other than the street, and the state must have something to offer other than force..Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: MOD objects to Yorkshire Dales wind farm plan over radar 'interference'
articles.summary: The Ministry of Defence claims the 200m high turbines would have "detrimental effects" on radar.
articles.body:
The Ministry of Defence (MOD) has objected to plans for a wind farm on moorland near the Yorkshire Dales, claiming it would cause "unacceptable interference" to radar.

Fred. Olsen Renewables is seeking permission to build 23 turbines more than 200m (656ft) high on land between Arkengarthdale and Teesdale.

The MOD stated it would also cause a "physical obstruction" to low-flying aircraft.

The renewable energy developer said it was working with the MOD, other stakeholders and the local community to address potential impacts and find "practical solutions where needed".

The MOD raised its concerns about the size and location of the proposed wind farm in a letter to the national Planning Inspectorate.

It says the turbines would impact the Royal Air Force's (RAF) ability to "detect and deter aircraft" in UK airspace.

In its submission, the MOD says it would cause "unacceptable interference" to air defence radar about 67 miles (108 km) away at Remote Radar Head Brizlee Wood in Northumberland.

It says it would also impact the air traffic control radar about 19 miles away (30 km) at RAF Leeming.

It adds that it would create "false radar returns" and also result in real aircraft "not being detected".

It also warns that the turbines would be in an RAF low-flying area.

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero ended the ban on new onshore wind farms when Labour came to power in 2024.

That meant that wind farms were prioritised as a Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project.

The government said its strategy for easing planning rules was crucial to achieving clean power targets by 2030.

The MOD has also objected to proposals for a wind farm in the East Yorkshire Wolds , claiming it would impact air defences and jet pilot training exercises.

Local people have voiced their concerns over the proposal, with campaigners calling it the "devastating industrialisation" of Yorkshire Dales moorland.

Councillor Angus Thompson, who has helped to lead the campaign against the wind farm, said that the MOD's "stark warning is the nail in the coffin for this scheme".

"The MOD considers that these monster turbines threaten national security and the lives of pilots," he said.

"This hopeless project should be abandoned without delay."

The developer argues the scheme could generate enough renewable electricity to power about 135,000 homes while helping meet climate targets.

Euan Hutchison, UK development director at Fred. Olsen Renewables, said Hope Moor could help in reducing reliance on imported energy and deliver a more secure and affordable energy system.

"We also believe national security and energy security go hand in hand," he said.

He encouraged residents, businesses and community groups to submit feedback as plans for the development continue to be refined.

A decision on whether the development will go ahead will eventually be decided by the Secretary of State for Energy.

articles.title: Lucknow restaurant owner dies after fall from building; FIR against influencer girlfriend, aides
articles.summary: LUCKNOW: A 27-year-old restaurant owner died after allegedly falling from the fourth floor of Awadh Green Apartment near Balu Adda in Lucknow on Saturday.
articles.body: LUCKNOW: A 27-year-old restaurant owner died after allegedly falling from the fourth floor of Awadh Green Apartment near Balu Adda in Lucknow on Saturday.The deceased, Shiva Sharma, owned the Vande Mataram Chicken and Aangan restaurant chains and also operated a cafe. His mother has accused his girlfriend, Shraddha Dubey, a social media influencer, and her associates of murdering him. She alleged that he had been subjected to physical assault, intimidation and blackmail for several months. Hazratganj police have registered an FIR against Shraddha and several others.In her complaint submitted to Hazratganj police on October 10, Shiva’s mother, Ranjana Sharma, alleged that she received a call from Adil, an associate of Shraddha, at around 7 pm on October 9. He reportedly informed her that Shiva’s condition had deteriorated and that he was being taken to King George’s Medical University (KGMU).According to Ranjana, when she reached the medical college with other family members, the people accompanying her son showed them his body from a distance and fled. Doctors subsequently declared him dead.The mother alleged that Shiva had sustained multiple injuries and was wearing only underwear when the family saw his body. She expressed suspicion that Shraddha, her driver, her sister Rashmi Dubey, Adil and other unidentified associates had assaulted and killed him.In her complaint, Ranjana alleged that Shraddha had been harassing her son for the past four months, threatening to implicate him in false cases and damage his reputation. She claimed that Shraddha pressured him to remain in a relationship with her and resorted to blackmail and physical violence when he resisted.The family further alleged that Shiva had previously been assaulted and pressured into maintaining a relationship against his wishes. Ranjana also claimed that Shraddha had visited her shop about a week before the incident and threatened her over her son.ACP Hazratganj Rajneesh Verma said the circumstances leading to Shiva’s fall were being investigated. He said police had registered a case against Shraddha Dubey, her sister Rashmi Dubey, her driver, Adil and unidentified others, and that further action would be taken based on the family’s complaint.Shiva’s elder sister, Astha, told TOI that Shraddha had been harassing her brother for several days. articles.title: Nine people killed in Pennsylvania shooting; suspected gunman found dead: report
articles.summary: Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah called the Perry Street mass shooting the worst scene he has encountered in nearly three decades of law enforcement.
articles.body: Authorities confirmed nine people are dead following a shooting in Pennsylvania Friday night, including the suspected gunman, who reportedly died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Police responded to a home just before 5 p.m. local time after witnesses reported seeing a person firing a weapon before entering the house, according to a report from Fox8 Live. The officers arrived on scene shortly after receiving an alert from the ShotSpotter app, the Erie Police Department said in a statement. Erie Police also said all shots were fired before they arrived and that no shots were fired after they reached the scene. Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah described the scene as the worst he had encountered in nearly three decades in law enforcement, telling local media that investigators were still trying to determine exactly what happened. "I want to be candid with our community. This is one of the most difficult and heartbreaking scenes our officers and investigators have ever encountered. The loss of life is devastating, and the circumstances we are working through are deeply disturbing," Lorah said, according to Fox8. POLICE REVEAL NEW DETAILS ABOUT GUNMAN, 5 VICTIMS KILLED IN RURAL MICHIGAN SHOOTING RAMPAGE Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro issued a statement confirming the number killed during the incident while offering support to victims' families. "I’ve spoken with Mayor Devlin and offered my Administration’s full support following the tragic mass shooting in Erie last night — killing nine of our fellow Pennsylvanians," Shapiro wrote in a Saturday morning post on X. "My heart breaks for this family. Lori and I are praying for their loved ones and the entire Erie community," he concluded. WFXP reported that the Erie SWAT team and numerous police officers surrounded the home before obtaining a warrant and entering the property. "It's a horrific scene," Lorah told the station. "There was a large loss of life inside that residence and outside that residence. … I can tell you that this is a tragic, tragic situation." MULTIPLE PEOPLE KILLED IN SHOOTING AT IDAHO IN-N-OUT RESTAURANT, SUSPECT DEAD Lorah told the station that the suspected shooter was found dead from a self-inflicted gunshot wound. The city of Erie issued a statement about the shooting, saying the incident resulted in "multiple deaths" and confirming that there was no ongoing threat to the public. "We understand that this news brings deep shock and sorrow to our residents, and we want to assure the public that the situation has been contained," the city said. "Our thoughts are with the victims, their loved ones, and everyone impacted by tonight's tragedy," the statement continued. "We will continue working closely with our Erie Police Dept, and will provide updates as soon as verified information becomes available." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Erie police told Fox News Digital that investigators were still processing the crime scene and that Lorah was expected to provide an update Saturday morning. The department's Criminal Investigations Division continues to investigate the shooting. This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

articles.body: An American Airlines transatlantic flight had to divert because six lavatories stopped working mid-air. American Airlines flight 37 was traveling from Madrid, Spain, to Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport on October 6 when it diverted to New York's John F Kennedy International Airport. The restroom problem was discussed between the cockpit and air traffic control as the flight requested permission to land. When a controller asked why the aircraft needed to divert, the pilot reported that only two lavatories remained operational.“You said only two potties, is that right?” the controller asked. “That’s affirmative,” the pilot responded.The conversation was sourced from LiveATC.net, a website that streams air traffic control communications.An American Airlines spokesperson confirmed the diversion to US media and asserted that it was indeed an issue with the aircraft's lavatories. “On Oct. 6, American Airlines flight 37, with service from Madrid (MAD) to Dallas Fort Worth (DFW), diverted to New York (JFK) due to an issue with the aircraft’s lavatories,” the spokesperson said to Fox News.The aircraft landed at JFK, underwent an inspection and then departed from DFW again. “We never want to disrupt our customers’ travel plans and apologize for the inconvenience," the spokesperson added.Though the reason for diversion may sound frivolous, aviation expert Steven Arroyo told Fox News that long lines for the restroom can present a security protocol problem and also lead to situations where passengers have to stay in line though the seat belt sign is turned on.“Being an international flight, the pilots, in coordination with the airline, would need to divert to a USA gateway airport that has customs and immigration services — such as a JFK, EWR, PHL, BOS,” he continued. That would then allow “maintenance personnel to board and fix the plane.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘Is peacefully raising your voice a crime?’ CJP alleges Delhi Police dragged, forcibly detained protesters
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on Saturday accused Delhi Police of forcibly detaining its activists and dragging protesters attempting to
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on Saturday accused Delhi Police of forcibly detaining its activists and dragging protesters attempting to reach Jantar Mantar for a demonstration demanding Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls.More than 7,000 people were detained across the national capital, while six police personnel were injured after stones were allegedly hurled at two locations. Police are also set to register an FIR in connection with the alleged assault on personnel.In a post accompanying a video purportedly showing police detaining activists and taking them away, CJP said: “CJP’S TEAM FORCEFULLY DETAINED!”“Delhi Police is pushing, dragging and detaining people for peacefully protesting!” the party wrote, adding, “Is peacefully raising your voice a crime now?”CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, co-convener Saurav Das and leader Ashutosh Ranka were detained aboard their flight after it landed at Delhi airport, according to the party. Legal affairs head Ratna Singh was also reportedly detained earlier outside her residence in New Delhi.A video from the aircraft showed Dipke challenging the officers. “I have come to be arrested, arrest me ... I am not afraid of you guys,” he said. An officer responded, “No, this is not an arrest. Please cooperate.”Delhi Police had denied permission for the proposed demonstration, with reports citing the late submission of the request as the reason. The authorities imposed extensive security restrictions, with barricades and personnel deployed to prevent protesters from reaching the designated venue.The protest was called over alleged electoral-roll irregularities and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise, with demonstrators demanding Kumar’s resignation. Several INDIA bloc leaders and activists were also detained, including Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) national convenor Arvind Kejriwal and former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee.In a post on X, Kejriwal said, "This is worse than the Emergency. It’s official.. we are living under an absolute dictatorship ruled by Modi. Arresting cockroaches straight off their flight shows an unprecedented level of fear. PM Modi clearly knows he only won the election through vote chori and now he is hell-bent on protecting his fraud by completely crushing democracy. Gyanesh must go, but so must Modi.."Banerjee, detained with Trinamool Congress leaders after staging a sit-in, also echoed: “This has gone beyond an Emergency; it has become a Super Emergency.”Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi expressed solidarity with the protesters and challenged Prime Minister Narendra Modi to detain all those participating. “Arrest all the leaders. Arrest all the young people. Arrest us all,” Gandhi said.The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), meanwhile, criticised the protest. Party leader Sambit Patra described it as a “flop show” and called the detentions a victory of democracy over “mob rule”.A police officer said six personnel were injured, with stones allegedly thrown at security personnel at two locations. The injured were taken to nearby hospitals, and the circumstances surrounding their injuries were being ascertained.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2024, 23-year-old woman died during wisdom tooth removal in Canada. Two years later, her father sues dentist, seeks funeral expenses
articles.summary: A 23-year-old woman died after undergoing a wisdom tooth extraction at a dental clinic in Canada, and her family has now filed a lawsuit alleging
articles.body: A 23-year-old woman died after undergoing a wisdom tooth extraction at a dental clinic in Canada, and her family has now filed a lawsuit alleging negligence by the dentist and the clinic.Virginia Blatz died on November 27, 2024, after visiting Boundary Trails Dental Centre in Morden, Manitoba, for the procedure. Her father, Dulaney Blatz, filed a statement of claim on behalf of her estate in Manitoba’s Court of King’s Bench on September 29, naming dentist Ronald David Janz, his dental corporation and the corporation operating the clinic as defendants.According to the lawsuit, Virginia was given medication to prepare for the procedure before receiving a local anaesthetic administered by Janz at around 9:20 am. The filing alleges that within minutes, she experienced two brief episodes of tonic-clonic seizures before she stopped breathing and her pulse became undetectable. An ambulance was called, and she was taken to a nearby health centre, where she was pronounced dead.An autopsy reportedly determined that Virginia died from local anaesthetic systemic toxicity after the medication was inadvertently injected into a blood vessel, according to reporting by the Winnipeg Free Press and CTV News.What does the lawsuit allege?The lawsuit alleges that the dentist’s treatment and management of Virginia’s care were negligent and caused or materially contributed to her death.Among the alleged failures listed in the court filing are injecting the anaesthetic into a blood vessel rather than the intended tissue, failing to check for blood by pulling back on the syringe plunger before administering the medication, and using an allegedly excessive dose.The claim also alleges that the dentist failed to adequately account for the risks associated with the medications used, recognise and respond appropriately to signs of anaesthetic toxicity, and administer or promptly initiate lipid emulsion therapy, a treatment used in certain cases of local anaesthetic toxicity.The clinic is also accused of negligence. The lawsuit alleges that it failed to ensure adequate staff training, maintain appropriate emergency protocols and have the necessary antidote treatment and oxygen readily available.The family is seeking damages under Manitoba’s Fatal Accidents Act, along with funeral-related expenses and other costs.Dentist faces restrictions on administering anaestheticAccording to the Manitoba Dental Association’s public registry, Janz has been licensed as a dentist since 2015. The registry lists restrictions requiring him to administer local anaesthetic only under supervision, along with restrictions relating to sedation services.The case comes as Virginia’s family continues to seek answers about the circumstances surrounding her death. The family had previously raised concerns about the pace and transparency of the Manitoba Dental Association’s investigation into the incident.The allegations in the civil lawsuit have not been proven in court. At the time of the reports, the defendants had not filed statements of defence.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Barlinnie visitors unable to use toilets as water supply problems continue
articles.summary: Some inmates at two halls first experienced problems on Thursday night and had no access to bottled water.
articles.body:
Visitors to Barlinnie prison have been unable to use the toilets as work continues to resolve water supply issues at Scotland's largest jail.

Some inmates at two halls in Barlinnie in Glasgow first experienced problems on Thursday night and had no access to bottled water.

On Friday the Scottish Prison Service (SPS) said the issue was proving more difficult to fully resolve and staff would continue to support people affected.

But the problems have continued into the weekend and one woman, who supports a prisoner, told BBC Scotland News that laundry was mounting up.

She said: "The laundry hadn't been done since before Thursday so the prisoners don't have anything clean to change into.

"They haven't been allowed showers either due to the water issue."

A Scottish Prison Service spokesperson said: "We are continuing to work with Scottish Water to resolve the issues being experienced in HMP Barlinnie."

Barlinnie prisoners face weekend without running water in cells

BBC Scotland News also spoke to another woman outside the prison who had been in visiting.

She said her loved one, a prisoner, had no water at all on Friday.

The supply came on again last night only to go off again later.

The woman said prisoners had been give two-litre bottles of water after initially being handed flavoured water.

She said: "It is ridiculous. It really should not be happening in this day and age."

The woman also criticised what she described as the "poor communication" with prisoners.

She said: "The visits are still allowed to go on but you can't use the toilet or anything like that.

The woman said prisoners often only saw their family for 45 minutes a week but were currently unable to shower in advance.

She added: "They are already in really tough conditions in there because it is so overcrowded."

The SPS said there were no prisoner requests for bottled water overnight on Friday but supplies were distributed.

It is understood that the prison reported a drop in water pressure to Scottish Water at 16:00 on Thursday.

BBC News was first contacted by a concerned relative about the water situation in Barlinnie at about 20:30 on Thursday.

At the time, the SPS said there was a low water pressure problem which was being addressed, but that there was no issue with drinking water.

One woman, who supports an affected prisoner, said that contingency measures should have been put in place immediately.

She said: "Surely distributing bottled water to prisoners should be an immediate priority when the water supply fails?

"These are not luxuries. They are the most basic necessities of life, and prisoners are entirely dependent on the Scottish Prison Service to provide them."

The woman said that she and others had contacted Barlinnie to raise concerns.

The SPS could not say how many prisoners had been affected but it is understood those in A and E halls had problems with their supplies.

A Scottish Water spokesperson said: "We can confirm there are no issues affecting the Scottish Water network in the area.

"The matter relates to an internal issue within HMP Barlinnie and we are supporting the Scottish Prison Service as it works to resolve it."

Last year the late 19th Century and early 20th Century sections of the Glasgow prison were recognised by Historic Environment Scotland (HES) as a Category A-listed building.

Construction of Barlinnie started in 1880 and the site opened in 1882.

It was the first new prison built in Scotland following the nationalisation of the prison system, with the Prison Act of 1877.

Barlinnie was known for being a notoriously tough prison, where prisoners carried out hard labour, breaking rocks from a local quarry.

It also served as a home for capital punishment, with 10 men executed by hanging at the site between 1946 and 1960.

In recent years the prison has been plagued by issues of overcrowding .

The Scottish government has committed to building a new prison to replace Barlinnie and construction is under way.

It is due to be completed in 2028 at a cost of nearly £1bn.

articles.title: Panama rattled by fresh 5.5 magnitude quake after powerful twin earthquakes
articles.summary: A magnitude 5.5 earthquake struck the Panama region following powerful twin earthquakes that shook the country’s southern coast on Friday, triggering
articles.body: A magnitude 5.5 earthquake struck the Panama region following powerful twin earthquakes that shook the country’s southern coast on Friday, triggering evacuations, damaging buildings and prompting tsunami warnings across parts of Central and South America.According to news agency Reuters, the European-Mediterranean Seismological Centre (EMSC) reported the latest tremor, while the United States Geological Survey (USGS) earlier recorded a magnitude 6.0 earthquake 7 km north of La Tronosa in Panama. The latest tremor came amid a series of aftershocks following the earlier major earthquakes.The USGS initially reported the first major earthquake at magnitude 8 before revising it to 7.6 and subsequently 7.7. The quake was centred about 10 km south-west of Pitaloza Arriba, a remote community in Herrera province, at a depth of 10 km.Multiple aftershocks continued to rattle the country, including tremors measuring magnitudes 5.8, 5.5 and 5.2. Seismologists at the University of Panama recorded more than 45 aftershocks, although many were too weak to be felt.“We felt it very strongly. It knocked things over in the kitchen, but we’re okay, though we’re very scared,” Rosendo Domínguez, 60, who is from Herrera province, told The Associated Press over the phone. “Everyone is outside, scared.”Panamanian president José Raúl Mulino said authorities had not documented any deaths as of Friday evening, while cautioning that the situation could change as assessments continued.“Nobody was ready, and no one is ever ready for this type of disaster,” Mulino said, after urging people to remain calm.Omar Smith of the National Civil Protection Service told Telemetro Reporta that damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera and Los Santos, with no damage reported in Panama City at the time. Several injuries were reported, including a person struck by debris from a partially collapsed structure in Penonomé.Officials also reported damage to the cathedral in Penonomé, the governor’s office building and the Dos Continentes hotel. Local media reported that the historic Church of San Atanasio in Los Santos province had collapsed.Tocumen International Airport temporarily suspended operations after the initial quake before reopening, while the Panama Canal Authority said operations were continuing normally as technical teams inspected facilities.The National Weather Service subsequently lifted tsunami warnings for several regional coastlines, including Panama, Colombia, Ecuador, Nicaragua and Guatemala.You use AI every day. articles.title: Christa Pike has been released from the hospital
articles.summary: Christa Pike is back in custody after being released from the hospital. She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, her legal team says.
articles.body:
Christa Pike is out of the hospital and receiving medical care in prison following a failed execution attempt.

Her legal team, Stephen Ferrell and Luke Ihnen from Federal Defender Services of Eastern Tennessee, and Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason from the TN Office of the Post Conviction Defender, issued this statement on Oct. 10:

"Christa Pike was discharged from a local hospital and is now at Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center where she has been housed for more than 30 years. She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances. She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery."

Pike's attorneys said Oct. 8 that she'd been able to walk after spending days in the hospital unconscious and intubated following her failed execution attempt on Sept. 30.

Pike's attorneys remain concerned about psychological damage and lasting impacts to her cognitive functioning.

The attorneys reported they were allowed to visit with her for the first time after she regained consciousness on Oct. 6. That was after they were already told by medical professionals on Oct. 5 there was a possibility she was brain-dead and would need to be taken off life support.

On Oct. 7, they shared she was confused and angry, still badly bruised on her arms, and had pneumonia and a blood clot.

Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 killing of Colleen Slemmer in Knoxville. The day of her planned execution, last-minute legal battles caused hours of delays. After the execution was allowed to resume, Pike was given two lethal rounds of pentobarbital, which she survived.

Emergency vehicles arrived as witnesses were describing what they saw and heard during the execution attempt.

Gov. Bill Lee is now ordering a third-party review of what went wrong and has paused the other execution scheduled for this year. Gary Wayne Sutton had been scheduled for execution Dec. 3.

The Tennessee Department of Correction, which handled the failed execution, said it did everything right.

articles.title: Trump throws another tantrum about not getting Nobel, declares war on Norway
articles.summary: TOI correspondent from Washington: Donald Trump has ended eight wars, or so he says, but he cannot make peace with the Norwegian Nobel committee.
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: Donald Trump has ended eight wars, or so he says, but he cannot make peace with the Norwegian Nobel committee. The US President threw an almighty tantrum on Friday night after failing to win the Nobel Peace Prize he has long coveted, declaring it “forever discredited,” and denouncing Oslo for an “indelible stain” on its reputation -- because it did not award him.He also dismissed this year’s winner, Navi Pillay, as a woman “nobody has ever heard of” and “I don’t know what the woman has done,” even as his administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying the move was aimed at ending the threat the “rogue court” posed to U.S. sovereignty. Pillay, a South African of Indian origin, has long been part of the international justice system.“I settled 8 WARS, am close to ending or settling 2 more… Yet, with all of that I, or the United States of America, did not get the Noble Peace Prize. WOW!” Trump posted on his “Truth Social” platform, misspelling the award, which is named after Alfred Nobel, not the adjective. This came after a ten-minute tirade at a rally in Syracuse, were he said rejecting him for the award reflects poorly on Norway and “those people that made such an disgraceful and embarrassing decision.”“We will not forget,” he warned NorwayIt was a monumental meltdown from a president who has spent years making sure everyone hears about how much he deserves the prize. But his tirades are now becoming the butt of jokes, with comparisons being made to a child overturning the dinner table because somebody else got the birthday cake. “Trump is beginning to resemble a jilted suitor who insists he never wanted the relationship in the first place, while checking the other person's social media every five minutes,” one wag quipped.The MAGA boss has been cultivating his Nobel grievance with the dedication of a schoolboy campaigning for head prefect, repeatedly claiming credit for ending eight wars -- including a four-day skirmish between India and Pakistan -- complaining that his supposed diplomatic achievements have gone unrecognised. Last year, he was reported to have phoned Norwegian finance minister Jens Stoltenberg to press his case, illustrating the extraordinary spectacle of an American president lobbying for a personal honour that is meant to recognise contributions to peace, not the persistence of its most enthusiastic applicant.He has also cited endorsements from foreign leaders, including Pakistan’s Shahbaz Sharif, for his claim. Just hours before the Nobel Committee announced the award, Sharief again fed into the fetish, posting on X: President Donald Trump played a historic role in advancing peace in South Asia. His timely intervention helped bring Pakistan and India back from the brink and secure a ceasefire, that is holding till today. In recognition of his outstanding contribution, Pakistan had nominated President Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize. We sincerely hope President’s efforts to promote peace and prevent conflict in our region receive due recognition this time.Pakistan had already announced it nominated him for the 2025 Award. Sharif’s last-minute reminder was therefore less a fresh discovery of Trump's peacemaking genius than another attempt to suck up to the MAGA boss. The Nobel committee proved impervious to the diplomatic equivalent of sending flowers before the results.Trump's disappointment is not new. Last year, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado gave him her Nobel medal, a gesture that apparently did not satisfy his desire for the real thing. FIFA subsequently created a peace prize of its own for him (dubbed the “Appease Prize” by comedians), but even the consolation trophy failed to close the gap between what he has received and what he believes he is owed.This year’s snub has also revived his antipathy towards South Africa, whose government he has repeatedly attacked over its domestic policies and its legal action against Israel at the International Court of Justice. Pillay, an 85-year-old jurist who fought apartheid and served as UN high commissioner for human rights, was an especially unwelcome choice for a president hostile to the international institutions with which she has been associated.Pillay, five years older than the 80-year old US Prez, was not entirely without a sense of humor about Trump the tyke. After receiving the prize, she joked that she might share it with him if the applause was sufficiently enthusiastic. It was a generous offer, though one suspects Trump would prefer the original -- in gold -- with his name engraved on it.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: King Charles warns malicious online actors are evolving their tactics
articles.summary: The King spoke of "threats to our international order" in a letter marking the 10th anniversary of the National Cyber Security Centre.
articles.body:
King Charles III has warned of the challenges disinformation and other "hostile online activity" pose to trust and security in the digital age.

The comments, made in a letter to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) to mark its 10th anniversary, spoke of "malicious actors" continuing to "evolve their tactics by using automated technologies".

"From threats to our international order, to the need to balance the risks and opportunities of powerful new technologies, strong cyber security is fundamental to making the online environment safer and more resilient," he wrote.

Last month, the King warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands.

In the letter published on Saturday by NCSC, the King praised the government agency. He said its achievements over the past decade have included defending the country against cyber attacks, safeguarding democratic institutions and protecting "the critical infrastructure upon which daily life depends".

"You have built resilience across our public services, businesses and communities, equipping us all to prosper in our ever-evolving digital world," the monarch added.

The King said he was "acutely aware" that much of the work done by the NCSC cannot be praised publicly and that he was filled with "profound gratitude".

The NCSC was established in 2016 as part of the Government Communications Headquarters to protect the UK against cyber threats.

Earlier this week, the NCSC offered assistance to online shopping store Asos after customers received a notification from its app sent by hackers, the BBC understands.

The high profile hack made global headlines on Tuesday when cyber criminals used Asos's own app system to send a pop up notification to potentially millions of people.

Asos said it was investigating "unauthorised activity" involving third-party platforms. The company told its customers that hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the company's users - including names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, customer numbers and dates of birth.

It issued the update after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.

The letter from the King to NCSC came after he spoke to AI executives at Dumfries House in Ayrshire last month on how the tech can be used to benefit security.

The meeting followed a series of recent warnings from people inside the industry about the rapidly evolving capabilities of advanced or "frontier" AI models and the regulation needed to keep them in check.

"Those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities - perhaps even to take life," the King told the executives.

He said there seemed to be an "urgency" in "adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways".

"The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world," he told the group.

articles.title: In 2019, The Miz and Maryse bought a 10,400-square-foot California manor for $6.4 million, renovated it during their ownership, and then sold it for $7.4 million
articles.summary: WWE couple The Miz and Maryse sell their renovated California mansion for $7.4 million, after purchasing it for $6.4 million in 2019. Discover the ups and downs of this real estate journey and their plans for the future.
articles.body: Celebrity houses often list at high prices and later sell for less. The latest example comes from WWE, where Mike Mizanin, known as The Miz, and his wife Maryse have sold the sprawling California manor they bought in 2019. The 10,400-square-foot home sold for $7.4 million, about $1 million more than the couple paid but far below the $11.995 million asking price in 2024. Variety reported the transaction in August 2019. They renovated it while they were there and the property was a regular feature on their reality show Miz & Mrs on USA Network.What they bought in 2019The home is in Westlake Village's gated North Ranch Country Club Estates. An English manor-style home built in 2001 on a 1.27-acre property. Variety reports the sellers were a couple outside the entertainment sector who paid exactly $6 million for the house in April 2018. A year later, the Mizanins paid around $400,000 extra.2019 listings described a nine-seat movie theater, a wood-paneled billiards room, a formal dining room with a fireplace and a large living-room fireplace. Around the same time, they sold their Texas property for about $2.64 million, which they bought for $2.35 million in 2017, according to Wrestling Inc. Miz & Mrs. had premiered on Miz & Mrs. premiered on USA Network in July 2018 as a spin-off of Total Divas, following the couple as they balanced parenting with their WWE careers.The long road to a saleThe house came with a large list of features. TMZ reported it entered the market with a custom pool and Jacuzzi, rose gardens, two detached guest homes, a recently remodelled kitchen, a private cinema, a wine cellar and golf course with mountain vistas. The pair reportedly underwent what TMZ called a significant refurbishment before listing.They tested the market more than once. TMZ reported that the couple had listed the property in 2022 as well. In September 2024 they put it up again at $11.995 million, saying they planned to move to Las Vegas to grow their business ventures. The couple's two young daughters were part of that move, according to TJR Wrestling, which made the sale a family decision as well as a business one.The deal was slow to get buyers. The sale closed in 2026, and their broker, Jordan Cohen of RE/MAX, announced the transaction on Instagram after what he described as a lengthy process. Wrestlezone’s report on his post says that once the proper purchasers came along they closed the deal in less than a week. Cohen commended the couple's restoration efforts and said the house had appeared on Miz & Mrs. many times. WWE referee Charles Robinson added his own joke, calling the massive property a “great starter home.” TMZ reported the sale on April 28, 2026, noting that Cohen had used John Cena's entrance music in his Instagram announcement.What the numbers meanThe $7.4 million sale price was about $1 million above the $6.4 million purchase price, a nominal increase of 15.6%. articles.title: Luke Bryan turned 150 acres of Tennessee cow pasture into Red Bird Farm with a bass lake, 10,000-square-foot home and 7,000-square-foot barn; the barn is now a haven for rescued animals
articles.summary: Owning a farm was a childhood dream for country superstar Luke Bryan, a dream that he chased even before becoming one of country music’s biggest stars.
articles.body: Owning a farm was a childhood dream for country superstar Luke Bryan, a dream that he chased even before becoming one of country music’s biggest stars. So, in 2012, when he came across a listing for a former cow pasture in Williamson County, he didn’t think twice. The Georgia-born singer immediately bought the 150-acre property just outside Nashville, Tennessee.Now, the farm is everything that a country home has to offer. Bryan and his wife, Caroline Boyer, transformed the rural property into what they call Red Bird Farm, with a bass lake, a 10,000-square-foot main house, a guesthouse and a party barn that shelters rescued animals. The couple now resides on the sprawling farm, and it is everything he dreamed of, and more.From cow pasture to country homeThe couple bought 150 acres of cow pasture south of Nashville in 2012. “We took 150 acres of cow pasture and turned it into something we couldn’t be more proud of,” the country singer told AD.Bryan had always wanted a lake near his home. Childhood dreams are meant to be fulfilled. So, once they purchased the land, they built one. “As a child, one of my biggest dreams was to own a lake to fish on. I thought that if I could ever have a home that sits on a bass lake, that’s all I would ever need to grow old and grey. Once we found out that the property could have a bass lake, we built one,” he told the publication. Caroline was equally passionate about their dream home. “Everything there is Caroline's and my brainchild,” Bryan said.Once the lake was dug, they were left with a large amount of rock, 140 tons to be precise. They knew they had to put it to use. So they used some of these stones for the fireplaces. Some went into a sunken courtyard. Others were used to build stone fences modelled on the old Civil War fences common in that part of Tennessee.Three main buildingsBryan named the property Red Bird in honour of his late sister. The farm has three main structures: the main house, guesthouse and a party barn. The couple hired Nashville designer Chad James to work on all of them, as they needed someone with a Southern sensibility.The main house, a custom-built mansion, spans 10,000 square feet. While it was under construction, the Bryans stayed in a 1,800-square-foot guesthouse, which has three bedrooms, two bathrooms and a stone fireplace. The double-height living room gave them all the space they wanted. The media room, kitchen and a screened-in porch were all built to their liking. The party barn, at 7,000 square feet, holds a golf simulator and a kegerator.Speaking about the barn, the singer said, “We trash the barn and leave the house alone. The barn also has these unique cobblestone floors. They’re great barometers of how much you’ve had to drink. If you fall on the cobblestones, you’ve had too many. I have a golf simulator and kegerator there, and it’s where I smoke my cigars.” A path outside leads to a catfish pond.The farm now has a rescue spaceBrett's Barn is now a safe haven for animals. Named after Caroline's niece, Sadie Brett Boyer, who died at seven months old from congenital heart disease in 2017, the barn is part of the Brett Boyer Foundation, which the couple established in her memory.The barn is dedicated entirely to rescued animals. One of its best-known residents is a white pony named Kilo, adopted in Sadie's honour. The number of animal guests on the property keeps changing. “A new animal shows up, like, every day,” Bryan said during his appearance on Live with Kelly and Ryan. The guests include donkeys, pigs, turkeys, llamas and miniature goats.Some of the animals arrive through local rescue groups. In 2019, Nashville-based Proverbs 12:10 Animal Rescue took in an 18-year-old dog named Poochie after his former family developed allergies. Bryan learned about this online, and they adopted him. Bryan has also said he is not sure how many animals live there.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 1935, Pennsylvania saw crown vetch survive on 10 acres of poor soil, so officials pushed it for erosion control and mine reclamation; it later spread to 46 states
articles.summary: Discover the journey of crown vetch from a resilient ground cover discovered in Pennsylvania to a widely used erosion control plant, and its troubling transformation into a nonnative invasive species across 46 states.
articles.body: Pennsylvania extension agronomist Fred Grau came across crown vetch that was across more than 10 acres of poor-quality soil in 1935. The plant had survived in an area little else could grow, with Grau beginning to study it as a possible ground cover, and within two decades, crown vetch was being planted extensively for erosion control and revegetation across North America.The discovery happened near Reading, Pennsylvania, where Grau found the plant growing on harsh cinder and shale soil. The Pennsylvania State University account says that the plant apparently entered the country as a contaminant in European alfalfa seed, and the farmer who owned the land called it “dot veed” because it kept returning after cultivation. Grau collected seed and took it back to Penn State, where he and colleagues identified the plant as crown vetch, and his work eventually produced the Penngift variety, which was named using “Penn” for Pennsylvania and “Gift” for farmer Robert Gift. Penn State records list the release of Penngift crown vetch in 1953.Highways became one of its biggest usesCrown vetch was particularly suited to the steep, infertile slopes that were created by road construction, and spreads through creeping stems and can establish on soils that have relatively low fertility, which makes it useful where it was difficult to maintain conventional grass cover. Penn State's roadside vegetation research says that crown vetch was first used on Pennsylvania roadsides in 1948, and wider operational use began in the 1950s. Thousands of acres were eventually planted during construction of the interstate highway system, and on Interstate 80 alone, Penn State estimates that almost 6,500 acres were planted with crown vetch.The plant was also used on mine sites, railroad embankments, and other disturbed ground, with the USDA Forest Service saying that crown vetch was widely used for roadside cuts and mining sites and became abundant in the eastern United States by the 1960s. Federal reclamation requirements later increased demand for fast-growing perennial ground cover on abandoned mine lands. Its usefulness came from its ability to establish quickly and persist under difficult conditions, but that same persistence eventually created problems.The ground cover did not always stay where it was plantedCrown vetch is now classified by the USDA Forest Service as a nonnative invasive plant, and it occurs throughout the contiguous United States and in southern Canada, although its distribution is especially concentrated around places where it was planted. The Forest Service records several examples of the plant spreading beyond its original planting areas, such as in Indiana, where a 10-foot stretch of roadside that is seeded with crown vetch expanded to about 75 feet within 10 years, and in Michigan's Ottawa National Forest, where the plant occupied 0.4 acres across four sites in 2003. Two years later, it was present on 14 sites covering 11 acres.Penn State researchers later documented another problem, which was that the crown vetch planted along roads could spread when soil was moved during construction and maintenance. Its hard seeds can remain viable for years, while its creeping root system can expand outward from established plants. The Forest Service now notes that dense crown vetch can limit the establishment of native herbs, shrubs and trees. Crown vetch went from trace amounts in 2003 to covering 46% of the area by 2005 on one Iowa restoration site, and the restoration project was abandoned. The Pennsylvania discovery had begun with a plant that could survive where other vegetation struggled, and the same characteristic that made crown vetch useful for erosion control later made it difficult to contain once it moved beyond the places where people had planted it.You use AI every day. articles.title: Eight killed in mass shooting at Pennsylvania home
articles.summary: Two children are reported to be among the victims in the city of Eerie.
articles.body:
A man has shot and killed eight people, including two children, at a home in the US state of Pennsylvania before appearing to take his own life.

Police were called to a street in the city of Erie on Friday afternoon after witnesses reported seeing a man firing a gun before he entered a home, the Erie News Now outlet reported. Two women were reportedly found dead in the street.

The gunman then barricaded himself inside as police surrounded the building and ordered him to leave, but more gunshots were heard, the outlet reported.

When police entered, several more victims were found along with the gunman , who had an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound.

The deaths were confirmed in a statement issued on Saturday by the mayor's office.

"Investigators have determined that all deaths occurred before officers arrived," it said.

"The deaths were not the result of any prolonged standoff or delay in police action."

Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said that "there are no words that can adequately express the magnitude of the loss of life here.

He added that police "will not speculate about a motive or any information that could compromise this investigation".

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said he had offered his administration's "full support following the tragic mass shooting in Erie last night - killing nine of our fellow Pennsylvanians".

"My heart breaks for this family," he said, adding that he and his wife "are praying for their loved ones and the entire Erie community".

The mayor is expected to hold a press conference on Saturday afternoon.

articles.title: In 2024, England protected a forgotten World War I practice battlefield; Browndown's trench systems span an area equivalent to nearly 17 football pitches
articles.summary: A conservation officer's discovery of a trench in overgrown heathland reveals a remarkable WWI practice battlefield in Hampshire, covering 17 football pitches. This site offers critical insights into the training of British soldiers before their deployment to the Western Front.
articles.body: An overgrown heathland in Hampshire has been identified as a First World War practice battlefield at Browndown Training Camp, near Gosport. The site at Browndown, equivalent to almost 17 football pitches according to a government release, contains two opposing trench systems and a no-man's-land. Browndown has been identified as one of the best-preserved and most complex practice grounds in England, providing evidence for how soldiers were trained before being deployed to the Western Front.The remains were brought to wider attention after archaeologists examined aerial photographs and conservation officer Rob Harper of Gosport Borough Council traced the remains on the ground. Aerial photographs dating from the 1920s onwards, including particularly useful RAF photographs from the 1950s and 1960s, helped establish how the remains had survived. Photographs from 1923 also independently confirmed their First World War date.The trenches followed the pattern of a Western Front battlefieldThe arrangement of the trenches at Browndown reflected the way British troops were trained to operate on the battlefield. The eastern complex comprised two opposing sets of crenellated frontline or fire trenches, and positioned behind them were the support, reserve and communication trenches. An approximately 130-metre stretch of open ground served as a no-man's-land, dividing the opposing systems. The surviving trenches measure more than a metre in depth, flanked by banks on either side that formed the parapet and parados. At the back of the systems are semi-circular platforms that are likely to have accommodated mortars or light artillery.By 1915 and 1916, practice trenches had become common at British training camps as the experiences from the Western Front influenced how soldiers were trained at home. But not every trench at Browndown belonged to these larger arrangements. Archaeologists also recorded more irregular trench complexes alongside simpler isolated trenches. The latter may have been used for teaching troops how to construct trenches, while simultaneously providing physical training and developing group cohesion.In contrast,the more organised system appeared to create an environment for soldiers to practise living and fighting under war conditions.Surveying the remains turned out to be difficult because thick vegetation, including gorse, obscured sections of the site. More ground for investigation was opened up between 2020 and 2022, owing to several gorse fires and deliberate vegetation management, enabling archaeologists to examine features that had hitherto been difficult to reach.The soldiers who trained there remain difficult to identify Despite the extent of the remains, identifying the units that used the practice battlefield has been elusive. The available documentary evidence includes a diary entry dated August 10, 1914, by James Thompson of the Plymouth Battalion of the Royal Marines Light Infantry, who marched from Portsmouth to Browndown to dig trenches.. Archaeologists believe this activity probably relates to the simpler, isolated trenches and doesn’t establish who used the later, more elaborate systems.The later trench complexes could have been used by the Hampshire Regiment or other regiments that were based around Gosport bound for the Western Front. However, the evidence at hand doesn’t corroborate the users of the systems with certainty, leaving the physical remains as the strongest evidence for understanding the usage and development of the training ground.Moreover, Browndown also holds remains from periods before and after the First World War. A round barrow, probably from the Bronze Age, a heavy anti-aircraft battery from the Second World War, along with interwar and later grenade ranges, overlap with the practice trenches. These overlapping phases of activity make individual features harder to interpret because several periods of use can occur in the same location.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
